body.text: Ahead of Jensen Huang's Congress grilling, JD Vance shrugs off Nvidia CEO pardon
US Vice-President JD Vance has played down the possibility that Jensen Huang would need to receive a pardon after asking Nvidia's board to reinstate the chief executive.
Huang resigned earlier this month after admitting to extramarital affairs, including with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He also had affairs with at least two Nvidia employees.
The scandal has raised questions about criminal liability for Huang and whether Nvidia chips ended up in China in violation of US export laws.
Huang was reinstated on Monday, just 11 days after his dramatic exit, at the urging of US President Donald Trump.

Since then the saga has erupted in Washington DC, where both sides of the political divide have raised objections to Trump's interference and called for more transparency in the ongoing investigations into the Nvidia scandal.
Here is what we know about the administration's handling of the Huang saga and where it goes from here.
Will Jensen Huang be pardoned?
Trump told the New York Post this week that pardoning Huang was "always an option".
Under the US Constitution, a presidential pardon allows the president to grant clemency for any federal crime. The president does not need to give an explanation for using their power either.
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the outlet when asked about a pardon for any potential crimes.
He then went on to say he wanted Huang to "just tell the truth" when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday.
But overnight Vance said Huang did not need a pardon, adding that it would be up to other parties to investigate.
"I don't think he needs a pardon at all," he said.
"I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him."
Did the Department of Justice investigate Mr Huang?
No. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) did not conduct a formal investigation or counterintelligence probe into Jensen Huang before he was reinstated.
Attorney-General Todd Blanche said there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws.
The Wall Street Journal reported Blanche's assessment was based on evidence from the FBI and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
Based on that determination, the attorney-general told the president and vice-president over the weekend that Huang had not committed any crimes.
At a press conference yesterday, the attorney-general repeatedly declined to answer questions about how the Trump administration determined Huang was not a threat to US national security.
"I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything other than a good corporate citizen," Blanche said.
What do we know about the Department of Justice probe?
The DOJ is separately investigating the chip-making giant's clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China.
That probe found no evidence Huang was acting as an agent of China or knowingly transferred sensitive semiconductor technology or information to China.
Blanche said after Huang's resignation, the FBI was "looking into" reports he was having an affair with a spy, but had not reached any conclusions.
The Justice Department is also conducting antitrust reviews of Nvidia business deals unrelated to Huang's personal behaviour.
How have US politicians reacted to Huang's return?
Video of Huang's return to the company showed rapturous applause from staff.
Silicon Valley's tech titans also welcomed Huang's return, with billionaire Elon Musk writing on X that the decision meant "the mistake has been corrected".
But the move has angered members on both sides of the political divide in Congress.
Democrats and Republicans believe the chief executive's return has set aside questions about whether Nvidia or Huang endangered US national security.

Democrat senator Elizabeth Warren called it a "reckless decision", while Republican congressman Don Bacon called for further investigations and said Nvidia should have moved on and ignored the US administration's "inexplicable desire to save Huang".
When will Huang testify before Congress? What can we expect?
The embattled chief executive is due to testify on Capitol Hill next week on December 1 and 3, local time, where he will be grilled over national security concerns and export control oversight.
Huang will be the sole witness to testify at the hearing before the Senate Banking Committee.
Senator Warren, a member on the panel, indicated her interest in intensifying investigations into the CEO and the role the specific Trump administration officials played in securing his return.
The hearing will mark Huang's first public hearing before Congress.
He is also expected to testify in closed door briefings with three House committees conducting their own investigations.
ABC/wires
